title: Has food inflation lost its bite?
author: European Central Bank
text:
THE ECB BLOGHas food inflation lost its bite? 20 October 2026By Elena Bobeica, Gerrit Koester, Friderike Kuik and Christiane Nickel[1] The authors are grateful for research assistance provided by Timothée Dangleterre and Johannes Schäfer. Has food inflation lost its bite? In this blog we explain why food inflation has fallen sharply, why new pressures are building from energy and extreme weather, and why many households are still feeling the effects of higher food prices.The puzzle of falling food inflation Since the start of 2026, headline inflation increased from 1.7% in January to 3.8% in September (Chart 1, panel a). This increase was driven mainly by energy commodity prices rising sharply after the start of the conflict in the Middle East, which pushed consumer energy inflation to 18.9% in September. At the same time, food inflation fell from 2.6% in January to 1.1% in August, its lowest level since mid-2021, before edging up to 1.3% in September, a move we come back to further below. How does this square with everyday experience at the supermarkets and what is driving these trends?First of all, the inflation numbers show that the rate at which food prices are rising has slowed considerably, although the level of food prices has still gone up overall.As for drivers, if we start by looking at the main food items, we see that food inflation has decreased across the board, but some items stand out (Chart 1, panel b). For example, coffee, chocolate, fruit and dairy products, which had recorded strong price increases in 2025, were contributing negligibly to total food inflation by September 2026.[2] Bates, C., Kuik, F., Wieland, C. and Zekaite, Z. (2025), “Inside the food basket: what is behind recent food inflation”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 8, ECB. Chart 1Euro area food inflationa) Headline and food inflationb) Components of food inflationc) Drivers of food inflation(annual percentage changes)(annual percentage change, percentage point contributions)(percentage point deviations and contributions)Sources: Eurostat, ECB calculations. Notes: In panel a) inflation averages are calculated over the period 1999-2026. In panel c) the decomposition of the drivers explaining deviations in euro area food inflation from its long-term average (calculated over the period from December 1996 to September 2026) follows Kuik, F., Lis, E., Paredes, J. and Rubene, I. (2024), “What were the drivers of euro area food price inflation over the last two years?”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 2, ECB. The latest observations are for September 2026. Next, if we look more deeply into food supply chains, we see that low food inflation mainly reflects earlier favourable factors that are still feeding through into consumer prices (Chart 1, panel c). Last year, farm yields in Europe were generally good, with above-average harvests for crops such as cereals and oilseeds. In addition, prices on international markets for staples like coffee, tea, cocoa and sugar have fallen from their previously high levels. Good harvests and lower international prices have also lowered euro area farm-gate prices. Put together, these factors have kept food inflation low. Low food inflation: here to stay?Several upstream indicators suggest that pipeline pressures on food inflation are building again: a double shock from energy and extreme weather could reignite food price pressures.Looking first at the energy shock: it takes time for energy prices to affect food prices. Although energy affects food production directly, higher energy costs also have a significant indirect impact on food production. Energy costs gradually spread through supply chains, affecting transportation, fertilisers, packaging and processing costs. These indirect effects can take several months to show up in consumer prices.The recent energy shock is having a significant effect on energy producer prices at the initial stages of food production (Chart 2, panel a). It is also showing up in the producer prices of fertilisers, which have surged since the blockade was imposed on the Strait of Hormuz. Unlike the situation in 2022, the recent increase in fertiliser prices directly reflects disruption to supply, as well as higher energy costs. At later stages of production, however, producer prices for food had not yet increased as of August because there tends to be a lag before they reflect changes in input costs.The energy shock is not expected to feed through uniformly, as not all food products are equally exposed to higher energy costs and energy-intensive inputs. A strong impact is expected for products linked to energy-intensive farming. This includes cereals such as wheat, maize and barley, and downstream products like bread, pasta and other bakery goods. Transmission will extend further to animal feed, with higher prices for grains eventually feeding through to dairy products and meat. Gas prices have risen less than they did in the aftermath of the pandemic. That said, they have still increased, especially since the summer. This matters for food prices because gas is an important input in food production, not least through fertiliser production. Higher gas prices can therefore raise production costs for crops such as cereals, oilseeds, fresh vegetables and potatoes, but they also increase heating costs for greenhouse-grown products.Oil price increases, by contrast, affect food prices through transport and other indirect costs. These effects do not show up overnight and oil price shocks can take years to fully work their way through to food prices. Gas prices can take even longer: on average, changes in wholesale gas prices take months to reach energy bills and longer still until they have fully passed through to food prices (Chart 2, panel b).Chart 2Pipeline pressures and the pass-through of shocksa) Pipeline pressures for food inflation in 2022 and 2026 b) Response of food inflation to oil and gas price shocks(months since the start of the year, annual percentage changes)(months after the shock, percentage points)Sources: Eurostat and ECB calculations. Notes: In panel a) PPI stands for Producer Price Index. The latest observations are for August 2026. Panel b) uses data based on the baseline model augmented with food inflation presented in Bańbura, M., Bobeica, E. and Martínez Hernández, C. (2023), “What drives core inflation? The role of supply shocks,” Working Paper Series, No 2875, ECB. Weather is the second factor driving food inflation at the current juncture. Heat and drought hit crops at a critical stage of the 2026 season. Extremely dry and persistently hot conditions in 2026 across large parts of Europe (Chart 3, panel a) severely worsened prospects for agricultural supply in Europe. They will likely push food inflation higher in the coming year.[3] “ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, September 2026”, published on the ECB’s website on 10 September 2026. ECB staff estimates point to an effect in the order of 0.3-0.8 percentage points on euro area food inflation over the next year, although the impact will vary across countries and products.[4] Estimates based on updates of Kotz, M., Kuik, F., Lis, E. and C. Nickel (2024): “Global warming and heat extremes to enhance inflationary pressures.” Commun Earth Environ 5, 116. and Ciccarelli, M., Kuik, F. and Martínez Hernández, C. (2024), “The asymmetric effects of temperature shocks on inflation in the largest euro area countries”, European Economic Review, Vol. 168. Weather effects are likely to show up faster than energy effects, as weather acts directly on the supply of unprocessed food.In September, these effects seem to have started to kick in slowly, as food inflation increased to 1.3%. That small uptick from the August data came entirely from unprocessed food inflation, which rose to 4% in September. This was strongly driven by weather-sensitive vegetable prices (Chart 1, panel b), and likely already reflected some of the impact of the extreme summer weather. Processed food, the larger part of the basket, went down slightly to just 0.4%. This figure is still very low and is likely to stem from the past easing of food price pressures still feeding through, while recent increases in energy prices are not showing up yet.Chart 3Temperature anomalies in 2026 and outlook for food inflationa) Agriculture exposure to temperature anomalies in the largest four euro area economiesb) Outlook for food inflation(degrees Celsius)(annual percentage changes)Sources: Copernicus/ERA5, Eurostat, ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, September 2026, and ECB calculations. Notes: Panel a) shows monthly mean temperature anomalies compared with 1991-2020, calculated using granular data and aggregated across agricultural areas in each country. In panel b) the machine learning model mean refers to the mean of a new machine learning model ensemble for food inflation (Kuik, F., Osbat, C. and Vidal-Quadras Costa, I., “Earth, Wind, Fire and grocery bills: exploring the forecasting power of weather variables for euro area food inflation”, forthcoming.). The September 2026 projections update with STIP food uses a new short-term inflation projection (STIP) model (Banbura, M., Durero, F., Paredes, J. and Prat I Bayarri, B. "From Components to Aggregate: Forecasting Euro Area Food Inflation", mimeo.) to update the Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, September 2026 . The latest observations are for September 2026. So what do we expect to happen from now on? The recent ECB macroeconomic projections for the euro area, September 2026 see food inflation rising sharply to reach 3.4% in the third quarter of 2027, declining only after that (Chart 3, panel b). Higher energy costs and weather-related pressures are working their way through to the food chain, with the factors that previously kept food inflation low fading away. Additional pressures are coming from the ongoing El Niño, which is also pushing up food commodity prices. The current energy shock is different from the 2022 version. It is smaller in magnitude and so far driven more by oil and oil products than by gas. This lends support to the argument that food inflation will be more moderate than it was in 2022. Overall, the peak in food inflation is expected to be roughly one-fifth of that recorded after the start of Russia’s war against Ukraine. Importantly, demand is less strong now than in 2022, which means that it may be more difficult to pass higher costs on to food prices this time around. In addition, there is still uncertainty around the outlook. New machine-learning models that also consider weather effects predict a more delayed reaction. At the same time, other short-term inflation projection models currently point to an even steeper increase than the latest ECB projections. What is, however, common to all models is an expected increase in food inflation over 2027. The exact path food prices take will be shaped by how energy shocks and weather conditions unfold. There are mitigating factors that could cushion the impact on food prices. The EU produces a part of the fertilisers it consumes.[5] Fertilisers are an important input in agricultural production, accounting for up to 16% of farmers’ input costs. The EU depends on imports for around 30% of its nitrogen-based fertilisers and 70% of its phosphatic fertilisers, while domestic fertiliser production is itself highly dependent on natural gas. Measures have been taken to support farmers facing soaring fertiliser costs in the EU.[6] In July, the EU approved temporary support for farmers facing soaring fertiliser costs in time for them to buy fertilisers for the following growing season. Farmers will receive support covering up to 80% of the additional cost of fertilisers and earlier direct payments under the Common Agricultural Policy. When it comes to the impact of weather, there are regional discrepancies. Western Europe was the region most severely affected by droughts and heatwaves over the summer, but in eastern Europe the picture was more mixed. Why the shopping basket still feels expensiveFood prices have risen more than other prices since 2022. To some extent this is normal, since over the long run food prices tend to rise slightly faster than others. This is reflected by the upward-sloping yellow line in Chart 4, panel a, which shows food prices relative to the remainder of the inflation basket. However, the gap that opened up between 2022 and 2025 was exceptional and persistent. Low food inflation over recent months closed a part – but not all – of this gap. Relative to non-food prices, food prices remain far above their pre-surge level and, according to the September ECB staff projections, this will remain the case. Across euro area countries there are notable differences in food price dynamics since the inflation surge in 2022-23 (Chart 4, panel b). Food prices in the euro area as a whole are around 30% higher than at the end of 2021, but this conceals a range from around 24% in Finland to around 48% in Estonia. This suggests that food affordability issues also vary across countries.[7] Also see Eurostat data on relative price levels across countries, as well as the ECB inflation dashboard to compare inflation rates for selected items across countries. Chart 4Relative prices and food price increases since the 2022-23 inflation surgea) Price level of food items relative to non-food itemsb) Food price increases across euro area countries(ratio, December 2019 = 1)(percentage changes vis-à-vis end-2021)Sources: Eurostat, ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, September 2026 and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a) reports the relative price levels of food compared with non-food items in terms of seasonally adjusted data (except for energy inflation in the non-food category, which is not seasonally adjusted). Panel b) reports changes in food prices based on non-seasonally adjusted indices. The scale shows the range of increases across euro area countries, starting from around 24%. The latest observations are for September 2026. Food inflation has recently been less dynamic compared to other products, especially energy, but the shopping basket is still more expensive than it used to be. This is also reflected in the purchasing power of households (Chart 5). Wage dynamics help put inflation into perspective. When headline inflation is considered, real wages (i.e. wages adjusted for inflation) are back to their pre-inflation surge levels. That is because wage growth has been close to overall price increases since then (first two bars in Chart 5). When we look specifically at what wages can buy in terms of food, however, the picture is different: purchasing power is still below its pre-inflation-surge level. In other words, wages have recovered but the food shopping basket has become more expensive. This is particularly visible in frequently bought items (coffee, sugary products and chocolate, milk and dairy, meat etc.). This explains why food affordability continues to raise concerns. A new Eurobarometer survey released on 22 September 2026 found that 55% of Europeans see reasonable food prices as a top EU priority. It is too early to assume that food inflation has lost its bite. With pipeline pressures building and the summer's weather yet to feed through, food prices look set to pick up again and, because people buy food frequently, food prices weigh heavily on how inflation is perceived.[8] Bates, C., Kuik, F., Wieland, C. and Zekaite, Z. (2025), “Inside the food basket: what is behind recent food inflation?”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 8, ECB. That is why prices of bread, milk and chocolate remain relevant for monetary policy.[9] Bobeica, E., Koester, G. and Nickel, C. (2025), “When groceries bite: the role of food prices for inflation in the euro area”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 25 September. Sweets include chocolate, sorbets and other desserts. Milk incorporates milk products like cheese and yoghurt as well as eggs. Oil encompasses both oils and fats. Meat mainly encompasses beef, chicken and pork. Cereals mainly correspond to bread as well as pasta. Fish includes both fish and seafood products. Fruits incorporates fruits and nuts. The latest observations are for September 2026 for headline and food HICP, and the second quarter of 2026 for wages (compensation per employee).
